analysis.one_liner: Phases out for-profit immigration detention and limits how criminal convictions drive deportation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled immigration enforcement. It would end mandatory detention for many immigrants, require a judge to presume someone should be released within days of arrest, ban contracts with for-profit detention companies, block state and local police from enforcing immigration law, and stop criminal convictions from automatically triggering deportation. It would also erase criminal penalties for crossing the border and let people deported since 1996 ask to come home. None of this happened: the bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants facing detention or deportation, asylum seekers, people with old convictions that today automatically make them deportable, and people previously removed from the country who would be allowed to ask courts to reopen their cases. Their families and communities, including U.S. citizen children of detained parents, also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a custody decision within 48 hours of arrest, a hearing before an immigration judge within 72 hours, and a legal presumption that a detained immigrant should be released unless the government proves otherwise.

Bans the Department of Homeland Security from contracting with for-profit companies to run detention facilities or monitoring programs, and requires all such facilities to be government-run within three years.

Ends mandatory detention for asylum seekers who pass a credible-fear screening and for many other groups, and requires judges to impose the least restrictive conditions and to set bond amounts a person can actually afford.

Removes many crime-related grounds of automatic deportation, narrows the definition of 'aggravated felony,' and lets immigration judges weigh humanitarian and family factors before removing someone with a prior conviction.
Repeals criminal penalties for improper entry and reentry into the United States and prohibits state and local officers from performing federal immigration enforcement functions.

Allows people ordered deported, or who left under voluntary departure, on or after April 24, 1996 to ask the government to reopen their cases, and requires the government to pay their transportation back to the United States if they qualify.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention companies and jails would lose federal detention and monitoring contracts. Opponents of the kind of changes in this bill argued that narrowing criminal grounds of deportation and decriminalizing border crossing would leave communities with less recourse against noncitizens with serious records, and that reopening decades-old cases would add costs and strain immigration courts.

drawbacks.text: Prior convictions could no longer be the sole basis for keeping someone detained, and judges could grant relief from removal despite a criminal record, which critics argue reduces protections for crime victims and communities.

The bill strikes crime-related grounds of inadmissibility, imposes a five-year deadline for starting many removal cases, and repeals the criminal statutes against improper entry and reentry — changes opponents said would make it harder to remove noncitizens with serious records.
The government would have to reopen cases going back to 1996 and pay transportation costs for eligible people to return, adding caseload and expense to an already backlogged immigration court system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real due-process protections — quick custody reviews, a presumption of release, affordable bonds, and an end to automatic deportation for many old or minor convictions — at the cost of narrower enforcement tools and a substantial new caseload for immigration courts and the Attorney General. The detention phase-out is unambiguous; the changes to criminal grounds of deportation are sweeping enough that honest supporters would acknowledge the safety objections were serious and the bill's reach went well beyond low-level offenses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its immigration subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuy Garcia introduced the New Way Forward Act on January 28, 2021 with 39 original cosponsors; 45 Democrats cosponsored it in total.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced.
On March 5, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Citizenship, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit detention companies keep their federal contracts and the existing enforcement framework stays in place; immigrants subject to mandatory detention and automatic deportation under current law gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit detention contractors and status quo enforcement

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 39 original Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 45 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referral to its immigration subcommittee; the bill never received a markup or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call to measure the split.

industries.industry: Private, for-profit detention and monitoring companies
industries.note: The bill bars DHS from contracting with for-profit operators of detention facilities or monitoring programs and requires existing contracts to end within three years, with facilities run by DHS or nonprofits afterward. These companies' revenue depends on holding people in immigration custody, which is the practice the bill targets.

The bill directs DHS to build alternatives-to-detention programs and lets it contract with community-based nonprofits for case management and supervision services, creating a funding stream for those organizations.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill prohibits state and local officers from performing federal immigration enforcement functions such as apprehension and detention, and bars immigration information from the national crime database. Agencies lose a cooperative enforcement role; the impact on the public depends on whether that cooperation is seen as public safety or as exposing residents to deportation.
